questions.q: What is the main goal of normalising a relational schema?
o: Remove redundancy so each fact is stored once and stays consistent
Make every query faster by joining fewer tables
Keep each table on a separate database server
Convert all columns to text so types never clash
questions.w: Duplicated facts drift apart and cause update, insert and delete anomalies. Normalisation trades some join cost for correctness.

questions.q: A table has a column `phones` holding "555-1234, 555-9876". Which normal form does this violate?
o: First normal form: values must be atomic
Second normal form: no partial dependencies
Third normal form: no transitive dependencies
Boyce-Codd normal form: every determinant is a key
questions.w: 1NF requires one value per cell and no repeating groups. Move phones into a child table with one row per number.

questions.q: In a table keyed by (`order_id`, `product_id`), the column `product_name` depends only on `product_id`. What is this?
o: A partial dependency, which breaks 2NF
A transitive dependency, which breaks 3NF
A multi-valued dependency, which breaks 4NF
An ordinary dependency that every table needs
questions.w: A non-key column must depend on the whole composite key. Move product details into a `product` table.

questions.q: A customer table stores `branch_id`, `branch_city` and `branch_manager`. `branch_city` is determined by `branch_id`. Which rule does that break?
o: Third normal form: non-key columns depend only on the key
First normal form: values must be atomic
Second normal form: no partial dependencies
Fourth normal form: no multi-valued dependencies
questions.w: That is a transitive dependency: customer to branch to city. Split out a `branch` table.

questions.q: Which anomaly happens when you cannot record a new product until someone orders it?
o: Insertion anomaly
Update anomaly
Deletion anomaly
Rollback anomaly
questions.w: Mixing facts about different entities in one table forces unrelated data to be stored together. Deleting the last order could also erase the product (deletion anomaly).

questions.q: Why do reporting or read-heavy systems sometimes denormalise on purpose?
o: It avoids costly joins on reads, at the price of duplicated data
Normalised tables cannot carry any indexes
Relational databases do not support joins at all
It reduces the storage taken by every row
questions.w: Denormalisation is a deliberate trade: faster reads against extra write work and the risk of inconsistency. Do it after measuring.

questions.q: What does 3NF informally say about a non-key column?
o: It depends on the key, the whole key and nothing but the key
It may depend on any other non-key column
It must be unique across the whole table
It must always carry an index
questions.w: A well-known mnemonic: the key (1NF), the whole key (2NF), and nothing but the key (3NF).

questions.q: A payments table keeps a copy of the customer's name for each row, so that old statements still show the old name. Is this a normalisation bug?
o: Not necessarily: it is a deliberate snapshot of history
Yes, it always breaks first normal form
Yes, it must instead be a foreign key to the current name
No, because names are never normalised
questions.w: Records such as invoices and statements should preserve what was true at the time. A snapshot is a different fact from the current name.
